extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students studying first-order logic (logic/CS/math courses)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, formation rules, and metatheory for first-order logic: syntax (terms, wffs, formation sequences, unique readability, main operator, subformulas, free/bound variables, substitution) and basic semantics (structures, satisfaction, validity, entailment, satisfiability), plus soundness/completeness remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressibility of domain-size properties
rubrics_metrics.description: What properties of a structure's domain can be expressed in first-order logic: one can express that the domain contains exactly n elements (for any n ∈ Z+); one can express that the domain is infinite using a set of infinitely many sentences; but one cannot express that the domain is finite, or that the domain is non-enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limitations follow from compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem theorems; use of infinite sets of sentences can express infinitude, but finiteness or non-enumerability cannot be captured in first-order languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness of a derivation system
rubrics_metrics.description: The property that if Γ ⊢ α then Γ ⊨ α is called soundness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soundness is a minimal requirement on any good derivation system: if the system derives α from Γ then α must be semantically entailed by Γ. Soundness is usually proved by induction on the structure of derivations (derivations are inductively defined and finite). If violated, the system 'proves too much.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of a derivation system
rubrics_metrics.description: The property that if Γ ⊨ α then Γ ⊢ α is called completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness ensures the system proves everything that is semantically entailed; it is harder to prove than soundness. Equivalently, completeness implies every consistent set Γ (i.e., one that does not derive a contradiction) has a model. Completeness answers which sets of sentences have models: exactly the consistent ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivations must be finite arrangements of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivations are always finite arrangements of symbols—perhaps a list of sentences, or some more complicated structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This finiteness is part of the definition of derivability (Γ ⊢ α requires a finite derivation). It supports inductive proofs about derivations and is central to soundness proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency, inconsistency, and models
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set of sentences Γ derives a contradiction (such as α ∧ ¬α) it is called inconsistent; inconsistent Γs cannot have any models (are unsatisfiable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From completeness the converse follows: any Γ that is not inconsistent (i.e., is consistent) has a model. This connection between syntactic consistency and semantic satisfiability is a core metatheoretic standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive formation of terms and wffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms and wffs are defined inductively: terms are built from variables, constant symbols, and function symbols; wffs are built from predicate symbols (applied to terms) and equality as atomic wffs, and then closed under ¬, →, and quantifiers (∀x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formation rules define the sets Trm(L) and Frm(L) inductively. This unique inductive construction enables proofs by induction and gives the basis for defining functions (like main operator) on wffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of primitive vs defined symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish primitive logical symbols (e.g., ¬, →, ∀, =) from defined symbols (∧, ∨, ↔, ∃, ⊤, ⊥); defined symbols are informal abbreviations and not officially part of the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing fewer primitive symbols simplifies the number of cases in proofs—defined symbols shorten proofs informally but are not treated separately in formal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique readability (unambiguous formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every wff has a unique reading: it satisfies exactly one of the formation cases (atomic, ¬β, (β → γ), ∀x β), and the pieces β, γ (when applicable) are uniquely determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unique readability ensures there is only one main operator occurrence and avoids ambiguity in parsing. Bad formation rules (e.g., omitting parentheses) would violate unique readability and break many definitions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main operator existence and uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: For every non-atomic wff α the main operator (the last/outermost operator used in constructing α) exists and is uniquely determined: cases are ¬, →, ∀ (with atomic formulas having no main operator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main operator is defined recursively; it is used to classify wffs and to name types of formulas (negation, conjunction, universal, etc.). The exact occurrence is intended (e.g., in ((δ→φ)→(φ→δ)) the second → is the main operator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of wffs by main operator
rubrics_metrics.description: Wffs are named according to their main operator (table): atomic (none), negation ¬, conjunction ∧, disjunction ∨, conditional →, biconditional ↔, universal ∀, existential ∃ (existential is treated as defined abbreviation for ¬∀¬).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined operators (like ∧, ∨, ∃) are abbreviations and not primitive; nevertheless one commonly refers to formula types using these names in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation rules for terms (formal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A term is either (1) a variable, (2) a constant symbol, or (3) f t1...tn when f is an n-place function symbol and t1,...,tn are terms. A closed term contains no variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constant symbols may be seen as 0-place function symbols; induction on terms (Lemma 62E) follows from this formation. Formation sequences for terms provide an equivalent bottom-up notion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation rules for formulas (formal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Atomic wffs are Rt1...tn (for n-place predicate R) or t1 = t2; if α is a wff then ¬α is a wff; if α and β are wffs then (α → β) is a wff; if α is a wff and x a variable then ∀x α is a wff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined operators and quantifiers (like ∃) are abbreviations; every wff is obtained at some finite stage of this inductive construction. Formation sequences for formulas give an equivalent constructive view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subformulas and immediate/proper subformula definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate subformulas: atomic wffs have none; ¬β has β; (β ∗ γ) has β and γ; ∀x β has β. Proper subformulas are defined recursively to include subformulas of the immediate subformulas. A subformula is α together with all its proper subformulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subformula relation is transitive. Proposition gives a bound: if α has n connectives and quantifiers then α has at most 2n+1 subformulas. These notions are used in many proofs and definitions (e.g., formation sequences, minimal sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation sequences and their equivalence to inductive definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A formation sequence for a term or formula is a finite sequence of L-strings meeting specified bottom-up construction conditions; every wff/term has a formation sequence, and conversely Frm(L) and Trm(L) are precisely the strings with formation sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formation sequences provide a step-by-step, bottom-up construction equivalent to inductive definitions, useful for proofs by ordinary induction on sequence length. Sequences may contain 'junk' (redundant elements), motivating minimal formation sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal formation sequences and occurrence criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A minimal formation sequence for α is a formation sequence of shortest possible length; a formula or term can have more than one minimal formation sequence but they contain exactly the same strings. β is a sub-wff of α iff β occurs in every formation sequence of α iff β occurs in a minimal formation sequence of α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimality eliminates repeated or irrelevant 'junk' from sequences; this characterization links subformula occurrence to formation-sequence membership and is useful in structural proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper prefix property of wffs (no proper prefix is a wff)
rubrics_metrics.description: If α is a wff and β is a proper prefix of α then β is not a wff (Definition 63B and Lemma 63C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property is used in proving unique readability: substrings that begin at the same place cannot be proper prefixes if both were wffs, preventing ambiguity in decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free and bound variable definitions; sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Free occurrences of variables in a wff are defined inductively (atomic: all occurrences free; ¬β: free occurrences those of β; (β ∗ γ): union; ∀x β: free occurrences are those of β except occurrences of x). An occurrence not free is bound. A wff with no free occurrences is a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scopes of quantifiers are defined; examples show occurrences may be free in the whole formula while bound in a subformula. This notion underlies semantics and substitution correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution rules and the 'free for' restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution s[t/x] for terms and α[t/x] for wffs is defined recursively. A term t is free for x in α if none of the free occurrences of x in α occur in the scope of a quantifier that binds a variable in t. α[t/x] is only defined when t is free for x in α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction prevents variable capture (example: substituting y for x in ∃y x<y would produce ∃y y<y). Convention α(t) abbreviates α[t/x]. The rule ensures semantic preservation, e.g., if ∀x β holds then instances β[t/x] (with t free for x) should hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structures (interpretations) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A structure A for a language L consists of: (1) a non-empty domain |A|, (2) interpretation of each constant symbol c as an element c^A ∈ |A|, (3) for each n-place predicate R (other than =) an n-place relation R^A ⊆ |A|^n, and (4) for each n-place function symbol f an n-place function f^A : |A|^n → |A|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structures (also called interpretations or models) give meanings to the non-logical symbols and are the basis for semantic notions like consequence, validity, and satisfiability. Examples include the standard model of arithmetic and many non-standard structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction relation and its properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction relation |=_A α [s] relates a wff α to a structure A and a variable assignment s; satisfaction is defined by induction on the structure of α using truth tables for connectives and the usual clause for quantifiers. For sentences (no free variables) the variable assignment is irrelevant, so one can simply say A satisfies the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inductive definition allows proofs about semantics by induction on formula structure. From satisfaction of sentences one defines validity (⊨ α), entailment (Γ ⊨ α), and satisfiability (some A satisfies all sentences in Γ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic notions defined from satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity: ⊨ α iff every structure satisfies α. Entailment: Γ ⊨ α iff every structure that satisfies all sentences in Γ also satisfies α. Satisfiability: Γ is satisfiable iff some structure satisfies all sentences in Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the fundamental semantic standards used to relate syntax and semantics (e.g., in the statements of soundness and completeness).
